newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan kicks off campaign for Oct 20 election.
newsitem.headline: Japan kicks off campaign for Oct 20 election.

text.p: Politicians visited rain-soaked constituencies across Japan on Tuesday, formally launching a 12-day campaign for the votes of an electorate which has only half made up its mind who to support.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, his own job riding on his Liberal Democratic Party's success in the October 20 general elections, told a crowd in eastern Tokyo that only the LDP could jumpstart Japan's economy and ease unemployment fears.

"Trust the LDP, and we will immediately get to work" deregulating the economy and streamlining the bureaucracy, Hashimoto said from atop a white party van as several hundred onlookers peered through umbrellas to see him.

Calls to cut back the bureaucracy, blamed for a series of scandals in health and financial administration, are central to the campaign pledges of all major parties, making it hard for Japan's 98 million voters to choose.

About half of voters polled by major newspapers say they are undecided. Only 52 percent of 3,000 voters polled at the weekend by the mass-circulation daily newspaper Yomiuri Shimbun said they would definitely vote.

Hashimoto, Japan's fourth prime minister since the last elections in 1993 broke the LDP's 38-year grip on power, also pledged to improve the welfare programme for senior citizens, whose meteoric growth carries ominous budget implications.
"We have a responsibility to do our utmost to create a society where living a long time is a good thing," he said.

Across the capital, Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) leader Ichiro Ozawa, Hashimoto's main rival, pedalled a "contract with Japan" platform of supply-side tax cuts and deregulation that appeared to borrow heavily from U.S. Republicans.

"I use the term 'contract' in the platform and this means if we assume power and do not carry out our pledges, I myself will take responsibility (and resign)," Ozawa told a large crowd gathered at a railroad station.
A day earlier, Ozawa mentioned Ronald Reagan by name while touting his plan to cut income and local taxes by 18 trillion yen ($162 billion) to stimulate the economy.

The LDP and Shinshinto are the only parties fielding enough candidates to capture a clear majority in the 500-seat Lower House. But most pundits predict neither group will do so and will be forced to seek a coalition partner.

A record 1,503 candidates are contesting the 500 seats under a new electoral system where 300 members are elected from single-seat districts and 200 by proportional representation in 11 regional blocs.

Yukio Hatoyama, whose newly formed Democratic Party is likely to be heavily courted by both larger parties, kicked off his campaign with a swipe at "low-minded politicians" who have talked reform but relied on the bureaucracy to stay in power.

The Democrats, made up of 50 young defectors from minority parties in the outgoing coalition government, are expected to do well in Tokyo and other urban centres where populations are younger and party affiliations fluid.
A resident of the Tokyo district visited by Hashimoto, however, dismissed the young Turks as lightweights.
"You've got to have political pros in there to deliver the goods and support employment," said Toshihide Iizuka, 75, a retired company official.
"Those young politicians make nice speeches but lack the weight to get things done," he said.

Ozawa's Shinshinto anchored its candidate list with the addition of sumo wrestling star Kyokudozan, following parties' long practice of running sports figures and television celebrities on proportional representation lists.
